title: Colours Through Time
subtitle: Arrange the events in chronological order.

subStages.question: Arrange the events in chronological order.
subStages.instructions: Drag each historical event to its correct place on the timeline.

events.title: Ancient Egypt's Invention of Blue
events.description: Egyptian artisans heated sand, copper, and limestone together to create Egyptian Blue, considered the oldest known synthetic pigment in history. It was used for coloring the skin of gods and the beards of pharaohs' statues to represent the heavens, the Nile, and rebirth.

events.title: Isaac Newton Discovers the Colours in White Light
events.description: Isaac Newton, working alone at Woolsthorpe Manor after Cambridge University closed due to plague, darkened his room, drilled a small hole in the shutter, and passed a beam of sunlight through a glass prism. He proved that white light is made of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet combined.

events.title: The White Wedding Gown Tradition
events.description: Queen Victoria wore a plain white gown for her wedding to Prince Albert, instead of the elaborate, richly coloured robes expected of royalty. Newspapers described the white dress in detail, and brides across Britain began copying her choice, helping popularize the white wedding dress tradition.

events.title: The Blue Period in Art
events.description: After the suicide of his close friend Carlos Casagemas, Pablo Picasso painted almost exclusively in shades of blue and blue-green for several years. Art historians now call this his Blue Period.

events.title: The Eight-Striped Rainbow Flag
events.description: Gilbert Baker, an artist and U.S. Army veteran living in San Francisco, hand-dyed and hand-sewed an eight-striped flag featuring hot pink, red, orange, yellow, green, turquoise, indigo, and violet, to fly at the San Francisco Gay Freedom Day Parade. Within about a year, the hot pink and turquoise stripes were dropped because the dyed fabric was too hard to source in bulk, leaving the six-colour rainbow flag recognised today.

events.title: Pink for Girls, Blue for Boys?
events.description: Psychologist Marco Del Giudice used Google's book-scanning database to search millions of printed books for the phrases 'blue for boys' and 'pink for girls.' He found the pink-for-girls, blue-for-boys pairing had actually been consistent since the late 1800s, contradicting the popular claim that the colours were once reversed.

events.title: Cricket's First Day-Night Test with a Pink Ball
events.description: Australia and New Zealand played the first day-night Test match in cricket's 138-year history, at Adelaide Oval. Since a traditional red ball is nearly invisible under floodlights, organisers used a specially coated pink ball instead, chosen after years of trials for staying visible against both grass and a darkening sky.

events.title: The Millennial Pink Trend
events.description: Starbucks released the limited-edition Unicorn Frappuccino, a pink-and-blue layered drink, for a single weekend. It sold out at locations worldwide within hours and became one of the defining products of the 'millennial pink' wave that had already been building across fashion, design, and Instagram since the term was first coined by New York Magazine.

subStages.question: Colors and their Stories

clues.clue1: It takes about 150,000 hand-picked, dried crocus flowers to produce just 1 kilogram of this dye.
clues.hint: For most of history this dye traded at nearly the same value as gold and silver by weight. Only three stigmas can be hand-plucked per flower, which is why the price has never really dropped.
clues.name: Saffron

clues.clue1: A dye-maker in 1704 was trying to invent a red pigment from crushed cochineal insects but accidentally created this instead.
clues.hint: The compound became an FDA-approved antidote for radioactive cesium and thallium poisoning, is stocked in nuclear emergency kits worldwide, enabled cyanotype blueprints, and was quickly adopted for Prussian army uniforms.
clues.name: Prussian Blue

clues.clue1: Dye-makers had to crack open roughly 12,000 sea snails to extract enough gland fluid to color a single garment hem.
clues.hint: In 2024, Paris Olympics organizers chose this exact hue for the running track at the Stade de France, the first time in Olympic history the surface was not red or blue.
clues.name: Tyrian Purple

clues.clue1: In 2023, scientists found that many walls at this ancient Roman site were never actually painted this color—it appeared by accident.
clues.hint: Lab analysis found the original pigment was yellow ochre, transformed within moments by superheated volcanic gas during the 79 CE eruption, inspiring the same colour on government buildings across many Indian cities.
clues.name: Pompeian Red

clues.clue1: A dye helped start a movement against the British Raj in Colonial India.
clues.hint: Colonial planters coercively forced Bengali and Bihari farmers to grow this crop for the European dye trade, sparking the 1859 revolt and later leading Gandhi to Champaran in 1917 for his first satyagraha.
clues.name: Indigo

clues.clue1: From the 1500s to the early 1900s, this paint was made by grinding up actual embalmed human remains.
clues.hint: Art suppliers sourced Egyptian mummies specifically to grind their wrappings, resin, and tissue into pigment for oil painting.
clues.name: Mummy Brown
